newsitem.title: UK: Italy gives EMU bond bulls an excuse to cash in. [CORRECTED 12:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Italy gives EMU bond bulls an excuse to cash in. [CORRECTED 12:20 GMT]

text.p: People who had bet on European bond yields converging dramatically this year can perhaps be excused for cashing in after Italy's re-entry into Europe's currency grid.

But analysts said on Monday the convergence trade -- which is part and parcel of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and has proved the most lucrative strategy in 1996 -- is alive and well. After a dose of profit-taking they say it will resume.
"The whole thing has got a bit of a 'Buy on the rumour, sell on the fact' feel to it," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in London.
"As we get closer and closer to year-end a number of players have done well on this trade (and will want to sell)," she said.
Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer in London, concurred.
"It's likely to provide an excuse for some profit-taking," he said. "But it (the ERM re-entry) really shows the convergence trade remains firmly on track."
Italy's move back into the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), a grid that sets fluctuation bands for member currencies, caps a year of fast-moving EMU developments.
As markets became convinced that Europe's leaders had the political will to push EMU through, investors swooped in on the highest-yielding bonds in Europe, such as Italian BTPs.
At the start of the year, 10-year BTPs were yielding 475 basis points more than benchmark Bunds. They currently yield just 170 more than Bunds.
After pulling out of the ERM in 1992 amid rampant mark strength, the lira went into freefall before finally regaining its poise in the past couple of years.
Finally late on Sunday, European Union (EU) finance ministers and central bank governors agreed to let the lira rejoin the ERM at a central rate of 990 lire to the mark.

One of the criteria for monetary union is that long-term interest rates in Europe converge, with no member having rates more than two percentage points (corrects from 150 basis points) above the best three members.
"This should ensure that the impetus continues. The mere fact that Italy has taken a further step forward towards EMU will have a knock-on effect for other markets," said Owens.
Spain and Sweden have been the other two main beneficiaries of EMU optimism. Spanish 10-year Bonos narrowed the gap against Bunds to a record low 128 basis points in early European trade.
Swedish bonds were yielding 139 basis points over Bunds.
Reed said bond investors for the time being were likely to use this as an opportunity to get out of BTPs and into markets such as gilts.

Gilts have lagged other markets this year amid uncertainty as to whether Britain would ever embrace EMU like other European nations. The spread of gilt to Bunds exceeded the BTP/Bund gap for the first time ever recently.
The 10-year gilt spread was at 179 basis points.
"We'll probably see spreads widening out. You wouldn't like to sell them too hard though," Reed said.
Italian bonds still have a number of things going for them, including falling inflation and the likelihood of further interest rate cuts, analysts said.
"The mood is still bullish, said Alfredo Granata, analyst at Banca di Roma in Rome.

Granata said the spread against Bunds would continue to narrow in line with the inflation diffential between the two countries. "We are going to tighten towards 160 or even as far as 150 in the next one to two months," he said.
Owens at Bank Julius Baer also had 150 as a year-end target.
Reed said the rate at which the lira re-entered did not pose a problem for the Italian authorities to cut interest rates as far as the 15 percent ERM fluctuation band was concerned.
"They could probably do exactly what they like with interest rates at that level, although shadowing 2.25 percent bands may make it tricky," she said.

Before the currency crisis of 1993 the ERM had two bands, one at 2.25 percent and the other at six percent. Then, after speculative pressure proved too strong for the grid to hold, the authorities widened bands to 15 percent while keeping the same central parity rates. Only the mark and guilder stayed in a 2.25 percent band against each other.
Reed said that the market was currently pricing in rates of around six percent by the end of 1997, which may be too optimistic.
